newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - EMU core scores well, Germany lags.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - EMU core scores well, Germany lags.

text.p: Five of the six countries expected to form the launch pad for a single currency are well on their way to meeting the required criteria but Germany may lag behind, a Reuters survey concluded on Wednesday.

Yet with economic guidelines expected to be brushed aside in favour of political considerations, the economic powerhouse of Europe was seen as being guaranteed a place at the launch of economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.

"EMU is first and foremost a political integration move. You need two countries to go ahead -- Germany and France. Without one of these, politically it's impossible," said Juergen Pfister, head of economic research at Commerzbank in Germany.
In response to the poll, which showed economists expected Germany to fail two of the Maastricht requirements, a Bonn Finance Ministry spokeswoman said: "The ministry expects to meet the criteria."

Reuters asked 32 economists across Europe to forecast the 1997 debt, deficit, inflation and interest rate yardsticks in the 15 potential member countries, to determine how they were shaping up for EMU.
The survey was carried out between February 5 and 10.
In the scramble to meet the criteria laid down by the Maastricht Treaty, Luxembourg was the only country to emerge unscathed, passing all the EMU tests with flying colours, the survey showed.
Austria, Belgium and the Netherlands were seen likely to fall foul of the total debt-to-gross domestic product (GDP) ratio.
With only three of the 15 European Union countries expected to meet the 60 percent or under goal, debt has become EMU's insurmountable obstacle.

Austria and the Netherlands almost make the grade, with debt for 1997 forecast at 72 percent and 76.2 percent of GDP, respectively, but Belgium is way over the mark at 127.1 percent, the median predictions showed.

France would escape this net, only to slip up on the budget deficit-to-GDP criteria. The target is three percent or less but the mean average of forecasts showed France over-shooting this year at 3.15 percent.
Germany is predicted to fail on both counts, albeit narrowly, with a predicted deficit-to-GDP ratio of 3.05 percent and debt-to-GDP at 62 percent.
With unemployment at a postwar high of 4.66 million or 12.2 percent in January, fears are growing that spiralling dole costs will cause its social security bill to mushroom.
This, combined with sluggish growth stifling tax revenues, puts the finance ministry's forecast of 2.9 percent of GDP in jeopardy, although it re-iterated this target on Wednesday.
"Because of higher unemployment than expected and lower tax revenues, a deficit below three percent is unrealistic," said Pfister.
But there can be no single currency without the mark and it is in the southern European belt, where interest rates are highest, that the incentive to converge with Germany is strongest.

"Most other countries in Europe have much more to gain from this project than Germany. The reduction in long-term interest rates is critical," said Sonja Gibbs, senior market strategist at Nomura International in London.
A Reuters poll of forecasts for EMU published last week put the chances of EMU starting on time at 83 percent, so some fudging of criteria seems imminent.
But analysts wonder how far the criteria can be tweaked to allow a core entry without opening the gates to the likes of the "Club Med" countries -- Italy in particular.

"Portugal and Spain will fulfil the new fudged criteria. At this moment they are not doing any worse than Germany and France," said Peter van den Houte, senior economist at Bank Brussels Lambert in Belgium.
